why_use_this:
Reach for this package when your data has more than 2 dimensions -- an image batch, a 3D grid of samples, a stack of matrices -- and [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s fixed rank-2 `(rows, cols)` shape genuinely can't represent it. A tensor here is just a flat row-major `Vec<f64>` plus an explicit `Vec<i64>` shape, with no hidden metadata and no wrapping struct, deliberately matching vani-matrix's own flat-`Vec`-plus-explicit-dims convention -- a rank-2 tensor's data is byte-for-byte a vani-matrix matrix, so you can pass one straight into the other's functions with zero conversion. If your data is genuinely 2D (or 1D), stay with vani-matrix -- it's the more specialized, more direct tool for that case, and this package's indexing/stride machinery is pure overhead you don't need.

A running example threads through the indexing functions below: a rank-2 tensor \(T\) of shape \((2,3)\) holding the numbers 1 through 6 in reading order -- \(T = \begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{pmatrix}\), stored flat as \([1,2,3,4,5,6]\).

tensor_size.intuition: How many numbers does a tensor actually hold? Multiply every axis length together -- a \(2\times3\times4\) tensor has \(2\times3\times4=24\) elements, the same reasoning as counting squares in a grid, just extended to more dimensions than you can draw.
tensor_size.example: For the running-example \(T\) with shape \((2,3)\): \(\text{size} = 2\times 3 = 6\) -- matching its flat data \([1,2,3,4,5,6]\), which does indeed have 6 entries.
tensor_size.why: Every other function in this package that allocates a fresh tensor (`tensor_zeros`, `tensor_ones`, `tensor_full`) uses exactly this product to know how big a flat `Vec<f64>` to allocate, before a single element is ever written.

tensor_strides.intuition: A stride answers "how many flat-array slots do I skip to move one step along THIS axis?" Moving one step along the LAST axis always means moving to the very next flat slot (stride 1) -- that's what "row-major" means: the last axis is laid out contiguously. Moving one step along an EARLIER axis means skipping over an entire slice of every axis after it.
tensor_strides.example: For the running-example \(T\) with shape \((2,3)\): \(\text{stride}[1] = 1\) (last axis, always 1). \(\text{stride}[0] = \text{stride}[1]\times\text{shape}[1] = 1\times 3 = 3\) -- moving one step along axis 0 (one row down) skips over an entire row of 3 elements. So `tensor_strides` returns \([3, 1]\). Sanity check against the actual layout: \(T[1,0]=4\) sits at flat position 3 (\([1,2,3,\mathbf{4},5,6]\), 0-indexed) -- exactly `stride[0]`\(=3\) slots after \(T[0,0]\)'s position 0.
tensor_strides.why: These strides are what `tensor_flat_index` multiplies a multi-index against -- get them right once here and every indexing operation downstream (`tensor_get`, `tensor_set`) works correctly without ever needing to know the tensor's rank at compile time.

tensor_flat_index.intuition: Once you know each axis's stride, converting a multi-dimensional index like \((1,2)\) ("row 1, column 2") into a single flat position is just: for each axis, multiply your index along that axis by how much one step costs (the stride), and add them all up.
tensor_flat_index.example: For the running-example \(T\) (strides \([3,1]\) from `tensor_strides`), find the flat position of \(T[1,2]\): \(\text{flat} = 1\times 3 + 2\times 1 = 3+2=5\). Check the flat data \([1,2,3,4,5,6]\) at (0-indexed) position 5: that's the value \(6\) -- and indeed \(T[1,2]=6\) in the original grid layout. Matches.
tensor_flat_index.why: This one formula is what lets a tensor of ANY rank be indexed with a plain flat `Vec<f64>` underneath -- `tensor_get`/`tensor_set` are both thin wrappers that compute this flat offset and then do a single array read/write.

tensor_unflatten_index.intuition: This runs `tensor_flat_index` backwards: given a raw position in the flat array, which multi-dimensional index does it correspond to? Peel off one axis at a time starting from the SLOWEST-varying (first) axis, using integer division to see how many whole "slices" fit, and the remainder to continue into the next axis.
tensor_unflatten_index.formula: Given a flat offset and the shape, recover \((i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})\) by successive division/modulo against each axis length, most-significant (slowest-varying) axis first.
tensor_unflatten_index.example: For the running-example \(T\) with shape \((2,3)\), recover the multi-index for flat position 5: axis 0 has a "slice size" of \(3\) (one full row). \(5 \div 3 = 1\) remainder \(2\), so \(i_0=1\) and we continue with remainder \(2\) into axis 1. Axis 1 is the last axis, so \(i_1\) is just the remainder, \(2\). Recovered index: \((1,2)\) -- exactly the index `tensor_flat_index`'s example started from, confirming the two functions are true inverses of each other.
tensor_unflatten_index.why: Useful whenever you need to iterate "for every element, what's its position" without nesting a nested loop per rank (which would need to be rewritten for every different rank you support) -- loop over flat positions \(0\) to \(\text{size}-1\) and call this once per position instead.

tensor_sum.intuition: Add up every number in the tensor, completely ignoring its shape -- a \(2\times3\) tensor and a \(6\times1\) tensor holding the same 6 numbers in the same flat order sum to the same total, because summation doesn't care how the numbers are arranged, only that every one gets counted once.
tensor_sum.why: Because this treats the tensor as a flat sequence, it works identically regardless of rank -- no special-casing needed for a rank-1 vector vs. a rank-4 tensor, one loop over the flat data covers every shape.

tensor_mean.intuition: The average value across every element, the same "sum divided by count" idea as an ordinary numerical average -- just applied to every number in the tensor regardless of which axis it sits on.
tensor_mean.example: For the running-example \(T=[1,2,3,4,5,6]\): sum is \(21\) (from `tensor_sum`), count is \(6\) (from `tensor_size`), so mean \(=21/6=3.5\).
tensor_mean.why: Built directly on top of `tensor_sum` and the element count rather than a separate implementation -- one pass to sum, then one division, rather than re-deriving the summation loop.

tensor_contract_last_first.intuition: This is what ordinary matrix multiplication looks like once you stop thinking of it as "rows times columns" and start thinking of it as "glue two tensors together along one shared axis, summing over that shared axis." For plain 2D matrices, the shared axis IS just "columns of the first matrix, rows of the second" -- ordinary matrix multiplication is the simplest possible case of a much more general operation that also works when \(A\) or \(B\) has more than 2 axes.
tensor_contract_last_first.formula: For \(A\)'s LAST axis matching \(B\)'s FIRST axis (both size \(K\)): \[ C_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} A_{\mathbf{i},k}\,B_{k,\mathbf{j}} \]
tensor_contract_last_first.example: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) (shape \((2,2)\)) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{pmatrix}\) (shape \((2,2)\)) -- \(A\)'s last axis (size 2) matches \(B\)'s first axis (size 2), so they can contract. \(C_{00}=1\times5+2\times7=5+14=19\). \(C_{01}=1\times6+2\times8=6+16=22\). \(C_{10}=3\times5+4\times7=15+28=43\). \(C_{11}=3\times6+4\times8=18+32=50\). So \(C=\begin{pmatrix}19&22\\43&50\end{pmatrix}\) -- exactly the ordinary matrix product \(AB\) you'd get from [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_mul` on the same data.
tensor_contract_last_first.why: Because this package's row-major layout means \(A\)'s data is ALREADY exactly an `(outer_A x K)` matrix and \(B\)'s data is ALREADY exactly a `(K x inner_B)` matrix in memory, this function doesn't need its own multiply loop at all -- it computes the right output shape and then hands the flat data straight to [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_mul_rect`, inheriting its already-tested correctness rather than risking a second, subtly different implementation of the same sum.
